definition: The mapped area inside the neatline where terrain, water, roads, symbols, and grid lines are drawn.
The map-specific instructions and metadata printed around the map body, including scale, legend, grid, datum, contour interval, and north information.
The border that separates the map body from its surrounding marginal information.
The identified publication or revision state of a map. It helps you judge how current changeable features may be.
The map-specific key that explains its symbols, colours, line styles, and abbreviations.
The mathematical reference framework used to relate coordinates to positions on Earth.
Canada's standardized system for indexing and publishing topographic map sheets.
The first half of a grid reference. Eastings label vertical grid lines and increase toward the east, normally to the right.
The second half of a grid reference. Northings label horizontal grid lines and increase toward the north, normally upward.
The area bounded by adjacent easting and northing lines. It is named from its left and bottom boundaries.
Two easting digits followed by two northing digits. On the course's one-kilometre grid, it identifies a one-kilometre square.
Three easting digits followed by three northing digits. It identifies a nominal 100-metre square on a one-kilometre grid.
The size of the area described by the number of grid digits. It does not guarantee that the map, observation, or plotting method is equally accurate.
A grid-based coordinate notation that combines zone and square designators with an even number of easting and northing digits.
The fixed relationship between a distance on the map and the corresponding horizontal distance on the ground.
A scale written as a ratio, such as 1:50 000, meaning one unit on the map represents 50 000 of the same units on the ground.
A printed line divided into ground-distance units that provides a direct measurement reference and resizes with a copied map.
The measured length of the path you intend to travel, including its bends rather than only the straight line between endpoints.
A personal count calibrated over a measured distance and used as one clue for estimating distance travelled.
A line joining points of equal elevation. Contours normally do not cross or split.
The vertical elevation difference between adjacent contour lines, stated in the map margin.
The vertical height of a point relative to the map's stated vertical reference.
The shape and height variation of the land surface.
The steepness and direction of rising or falling ground. With one contour interval, closer contours indicate steeper ground.
A long crest of higher ground with land falling away on both sides.
A finger of higher ground projecting outward from a ridge. Its contour bends normally point downhill.
Lower ground between higher sides, often containing drainage. Its contour bends normally point uphill.
A lower pass between two adjacent areas of higher ground. Lower contours may enclose both rises while higher contours separate around each rise.
The geographic direction toward the North Pole.
The direction of the vertical grid lines on the map.
The direction indicated by a magnetic compass needle.
The local, time-dependent angular relationship between magnetic north and another north reference shown for the map.
A horizontal direction expressed as an angle clockwise from a stated north reference.
One planned section of a route between two recognizable points or decisions.
A recognizable linear feature, such as a trail, stream, shoreline, or ridge, used to organize movement.
A recognizable feature expected along a route that confirms progress or position.
A clear feature close to the destination from which the precise final approach begins.
A feature beyond the destination that makes an overshoot recognizable.
A preselected observation, limit, or uncertainty that tells you to stop moving and reassess.
Rotate the map so its directions and visible features correspond with the surrounding ground.
The most recent point where reliable map and ground evidence established your location.
Correctly applying a skill to a fresh example without being led through each step.
